subtitleEn: The rest of Hangul, and the words it opens.
hoyaIntroEn: You know 30 letters. Let us meet the rest and read more words!

quests.blurbEn: Four new vowels: ae, e, yae and ye.

steps.hoyaLineEn: You can read 30 letters. Let us meet four more vowels!
Many people say ae and e the same way today. The spelling tells them apart.
Four new vowels, and so many new words. Well done!

text.en: older sister (said by a man or boy)

quests.blurbEn: Five doubled letters: kk, tt, pp, ss and jj.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Two of the same letter make one new sound. Let us meet five!

steps.titleEn: Meet kk, tt, pp, ss, jj
steps.hoyaLineEn: A doubled letter is said tight and strong, with almost no puff of air.
You read five doubled letters. Great work!

quests.titleEn: Joined Vowels wa, wo, wi, ui
quests.blurbEn: Four vowels made from two you know.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Two vowels you know can join into one. Let us see how!
Each joined vowel is two vowels you know, said quickly as one sound.
Four joined vowels read. You are on a roll!

quests.blurbEn: Three joined vowels that sound alike.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Three more joined vowels today. Their shapes tell them apart.
Today these three often sound almost the same. Learn them by their shapes.
You have met every vowel letter of Hangul. Well done!

quests.blurbEn: Six bottom letters that all end in t.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Six letters at the bottom of a block end with the same sound!

steps.titleEn: The t Sound at the End
steps.hoyaLineEn: At the end of a word, these six letters say t. When an ending that starts with a vowel comes next, the letter moves on and keeps its own sound.
Six new bottom letters, one t sound. Great work!

quests.titleEn: More Letters for k and p
quests.blurbEn: Three new bottom letters with sounds you know.

steps.hoyaLineEn: You know k and p at the end of a block. Three more letters make them!
At the end of a word, k and kk say k, as g does. And p says p, as b does.
You met the last new letters of Word Builder. Wonderful!

culture.textEn: In everyday speech today, most people no longer keep {ko:ㅐ} and {ko:ㅔ} apart, so the spelling, not the sound, shows which one a word uses.

sources.title: 표준어 규정 제2부 표준 발음법
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제2부 표준 발음법, 제2장 제4항 해설: "이상의 단모음 중 'ㅐ'와 'ㅔ'는 현재 대부분의 세대에서 별개의 모음으로 구별되지 않고 있다."

sources.title: 모음(母音)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 중부방언 단모음 체계 부분: "40대 이하의 세대에서는 /e/와 /ɛ/가 구별되지 않으므로 그 둘의 구별이 없는 음소 /E/를 가지게 된다."

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): both sources opened; the NIKL standard pronunciation commentary to article 4 says ㅐ and ㅔ are not kept apart by most generations today, and the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says speakers in their forties and younger do not distinguish /e/ and /ɛ/. Backs the q1 Discover Hoya line. The games never ask the learner to tell ㅐ from ㅔ by ear.
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): both sources re-opened. NIKL article 4 commentary says most generations no longer tell ㅐ and ㅔ apart (the article 1 commentary adds: most people outside some older speakers in some regions); the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture note to table 1 says Central-dialect speakers in their forties and younger have one merged /E/. Both quoted locators match the pages word for word. Claim holds; no wording shared with the sources.

culture.textEn: The five doubled letters {ko:ㄲ}, {ko:ㄸ}, {ko:ㅃ}, {ko:ㅆ} and {ko:ㅉ} are tense sounds: the throat tightens and almost no breath comes out, unlike the plain and the puff-of-air letters.

sources.title: 된소리
sources.quoteOrLocator: 표제어 '된소리'(word_no 92362), 뜻풀이: "후두 근육의 긴장도를 높이면서 기식이 거의 없이 내는 자음. 'ㄲ', 'ㄸ', 'ㅃ', 'ㅆ', 'ㅉ' 따위의 소리이다."

sources.title: 자음(子音)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 파열음 부분: "국어에 사용되는 파열음에는 평파열음(平破裂音) · 경파열음(硬破裂音) · 유기파열음(有氣破裂音)이 있다."; 경파열음 [p'], [t'], [k'] ('뼈, 딸, 끝'의 초성), 경무성마찰음 [s'] ('싸움, 씨름')

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): the dictionary defines the tense consonants ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ as said with raised laryngeal tension and almost no aspiration; the encyclopedia sets the tense series beside the plain and the aspirated series. Backs the q2 Discover Hoya line (tight and strong, almost no puff of air).
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): the Standard Korean Language Dictionary entry 된소리 (one result) defines it as said with raised laryngeal-muscle tension and almost no aspiration, examples ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ; the encyclopedia's stops section names the plain, tense and aspirated series (tense: initials of 뼈, 딸, 끝) and its fricatives section names tense [s'] in 싸움, 씨름. 'Throat tightens' is a plain-words restatement of laryngeal tension. Claim holds; no copied wording.

culture.textEn: {ko:ㅘ}, {ko:ㅝ}, {ko:ㅟ} and {ko:ㅢ} are each written by joining two simple vowel letters, and each can be said as one gliding sound.

sources.title: 표준어 규정 제2부 표준 발음법
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제2부 표준 발음법, 제2장 제5항: "'ㅑ ㅒ ㅕ ㅖ ㅘ ㅙ ㅛ ㅝ ㅞ ㅠ ㅢ'는 이중 모음으로 발음한다."; 제4항 [붙임]: "'ㅚ, ㅟ'는 이중 모음으로 발음할 수 있다."; 제5항 다만 3, 다만 4 (ㅢ의 허용 발음)

sources.title: 모음(母音)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 이중모음 부분: "'ㅘ[wa], ㅙ[wɛ], ㅝ[wʌ], ㅞ[we]'"; "'ㅟ[y]'는 마찰음 · 파찰음 이외의 자음 뒤에서는 대체로 [wi]로 발음된다."

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): article 5 of the standard pronunciation rules lists ㅘ ㅝ ㅢ among the diphthongs and article 4 lets ㅟ be said as one; the encyclopedia transcribes ㅘ as [wa], ㅝ as [wʌ] and ㅟ as usually [wi]. Backs the q3 Discover Hoya line (two vowels you know, said quickly as one sound); the letter shapes (ㅗ+ㅏ, ㅜ+ㅓ, ㅜ+ㅣ, ㅡ+ㅣ) are visible in the letters themselves.
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): article 5 lists ㅘ ㅝ ㅢ as diphthongs and its commentary builds ㅘ ㅝ from [w] plus ㅏ ㅓ and ㅢ from ㅡ plus [j]; article 4 makes ㅟ a monophthong in principle with a diphthong allowed, and article 5 provisos 3-4 say ㅢ after a consonant is said [ㅣ] and is allowed as [ㅣ] or [ㅔ] elsewhere. 'Each is said as one gliding sound' overstated ㅟ and ㅢ, so the note now says 'each can be said as one gliding sound'; locator extended to provisos 3-4. Encyclopedia quotes ([wa], [wʌ], ㅟ usually [wi]) match. Holds as revised.

culture.textEn: {ko:ㅚ} may be said as a gliding vowel, and since {ko:ㅐ} and {ko:ㅔ} are heard alike today, {ko:ㅚ}, {ko:ㅙ} and {ko:ㅞ} often sound nearly the same; their shapes keep them apart.

sources.title: 표준어 규정 제2부 표준 발음법
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제2장 제4항 [붙임]: "'ㅚ, ㅟ'는 이중 모음으로 발음할 수 있다."; 제4항 해설: "'ㅐ'와 'ㅔ'는 현재 대부분의 세대에서 별개의 모음으로 구별되지 않고 있다."; 제5항: 'ㅙ', 'ㅞ'는 이중 모음; 제4항 해설 끝 문단 (이중 모음으로 발음한 'ㅚ'는 'ㅞ'와 같음, 예: '회' [회]/[훼])

sources.title: 모음(母音)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 이중모음 부분: "'ㅘ[wa], ㅙ[wɛ], ㅝ[wʌ], ㅞ[we]'"; 제주방언 부분: /ø/는 이중모음 "[wE]또는 [we]로 실현된다"; 중부방언: 40대 이하 세대는 /e/와 /ɛ/를 구별하지 않음

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): ㅚ may be a diphthong (article 4, attachment), ㅙ is [wɛ] and ㅞ is [we] (encyclopedia), and ㅐ / ㅔ are not kept apart by most speakers (article 4 commentary; encyclopedia), so the three end up close. The note says 'often' and 'nearly', not 'always'. Backs the q4 Discover Hoya line; the games never ask for this contrast by ear.
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): NIKL article 4 attachment allows ㅚ as a diphthong and its commentary says diphthong ㅚ is the same as ㅞ (회 [회]/[훼]); article 4 commentary says ㅐ and ㅔ have merged for most generations; the encyclopedia gives ㅙ [wɛ], ㅞ [we]. So ㅚ ㅙ ㅞ come out close; 'often' and 'nearly' are kept. The encyclopedia's Jeju line is dialect-only, so the merger rests on NIKL; locator extended to the ㅚ = ㅞ commentary. Claim holds; no copied wording.

culture.textEn: At the end of a word or before a consonant a bottom letter is said as one of seven sounds: {ko:ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ} end like {ko:ㄷ}, in t; {ko:ㄲ ㅋ} like {ko:ㄱ}, in k; and {ko:ㅍ} like {ko:ㅂ}, in p.

sources.title: 표준어 규정 제2부 표준 발음법
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제4장 받침의 발음, 제8항: "받침소리로는 'ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ'의 7개 자음만 발음한다."; 제9항: "받침 'ㄲ, ㅋ', 'ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ', 'ㅍ'은 어말 또는 자음 앞에서 각각 대표음 [ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ]으로 발음한다."

sources.title: 자음(子音)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 파열음 부분: "이들은 음절말에서 각기 [p], [t], [k]로만 실현된다."; 파찰음 부분 (/ㅈ, ㅉ, ㅊ/)과 마찰음 부분 (/s/, /s'/): 음절말에서 [t]로 실현

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): articles 8 and 9 give the seven final sounds and the representative sounds of ㄲ ㅋ (ㄱ), ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ (ㄷ) and ㅍ (ㅂ); the encyclopedia says these stops and fricatives are realised only as [p], [t], [k] at the end of a syllable. Backs the q5 and q6 Discover Hoya lines. Final ㅎ is not in article 9 (article 12 gives it other rules), so q5 teaches six t letters, not ㅎ.
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): article 8 gives the seven final sounds ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅇ; article 9 maps final ㄲ ㅋ to [ㄱ], ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ to [ㄷ], ㅍ to [ㅂ] at word end or before a consonant (examples 옷[옫], 꽃[꼳], 앞[압]); article 12 treats final ㅎ separately. The encyclopedia says the stops surface only as [p] [t] [k] syllable-finally and the affricates and /s/, /s'/ as [t]; locator widened to name those parts. Claim holds; no copied wording.

culture.textEn: When an ending or particle that starts with a vowel follows, a bottom letter moves over to the next block and keeps its own sound: {ko:옷이} is said osi, not with a t.

sources.title: 표준어 규정 제2부 표준 발음법
sources.quoteOrLocator: 제4장 받침의 발음, 제13항: "홑받침이나 쌍받침이 모음으로 시작된 조사나 어미, 접미사와 결합되는 경우에는, 제 음가대로 뒤 음절 첫소리로 옮겨 발음한다."

sources.title: 표준 발음법의 이해 (한글 자모의 발음)
sources.publisher: 국립국어원 새국어소식 (National Institute of Korean Language)
sources.quoteOrLocator: 받침과 모음으로 시작하는 조사·어미의 결합 예: "옷이 [오시], 꽃이 [꼬치]"

verification.notes:
Pass 1 (author sourcing, 2026-10-14): article 13 moves a single or double final to the next syllable with its own value before a vowel-initial particle, ending or suffix, and the NIKL explainer gives 옷이 [오시]. Backs the second sentence of the q5 Discover Hoya line.
Pass 2b (independent fact check, 2026-10-14): article 13 (in chapter 4, Pronouncing final consonants, not chapter 5 as the locator said: corrected) moves a single or double final, with its own value, to the next syllable before a vowel-initial particle, ending or suffix, example 옷이[오시]; the NIKL 새국어소식 article (2001, June) gives 옷이[오시], 꽃이[꼬치] and contrasts 겉옷[거돋]. Claim holds; no copied wording.
